title: Why Consistency Is Everything The First Two Weeks Of The School Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns that the 'honeymoon period' of the first two weeks of school hides a danger: small, seemingly harmless decisions to let minor rule-breaking slide can undermine a teacher's consistency for the rest of the year. He gives concrete examples—answering a question asked without a raised hand, accepting a spontaneous lunch invitation that breaks a lining-up rule—and explains how these exceptions signal that the teacher doesn't fully mean what they say, opening the door to subjective, inconsistent enforcement. He argues students test boundaries in small ways early on specifically to learn whether a teacher is a person of their word, since many past teachers have posted rules they didn't consistently enforce. His prescription includes knowing precisely what does and doesn't break each rule, and a daily few-minute visualization ritual before school to mentally commit to following the plan exactly as written, like a referee, with no hesitation or judgment.

quotes: The first two weeks of the school year is the honeymoon period. Students are eager and wanting to please.
You’ve sent a message to the entire class that you don’t really mean what you say and have now put yourself in position to judge subjectively when and whether a student deserves a consequence.
You see, minor, seemingly harmless misbehavior in the beginning always leads to major disruptions once the honeymoon period ends.
So many students have had teachers in the past who post rules and consequences, but only kinda-sorta follow them. And they assume you’ll be like all the rest.
First, you must know precisely what does and doesn’t constitute breaking your rules . Because if you’re unsure, then you can’t possibly be consistent.
Visualize yourself recognizing misbehavior when it happens, calmly enforcing your plan like a referee , and then moving on as if nothing happened.
